items.title: UK GDPR, Article 33: Notification of a personal data breach to the Commission
items.quote: without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it
items.why: The binding reporting window where an AI failure is also a personal data breach. Notification is to the Commission (word substituted for 'the Commissioner'; see the notes on the page). Art. 33(2): a processor must tell the controller without undue delay. Art. 33(5): every breach must be documented. The page shows no known outstanding effects.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 34: Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject
items.quote: the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay
items.why: The duty to tell the people affected when the breach is likely to result in a high risk to them. This is the part of incident response that most directly protects individuals. No known outstanding effects.

items.title: Personal data breaches: a guide
items.locator: Sections 'At a glance', 'Checklists' and 'What breaches do we need to notify the ICO about?'; latest update noted 20 August 2025
items.quote: You should ensure that you record all breaches, regardless of whether or not they need to be reported to the ICO.
items.why: The regulator's reading of Articles 33 and 34: have a prepared response plan, a process to notify within 72 hours even without full details, and a record of every breach. No 'under review' banner was seen on the page on the date checked.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: Developers and System Operators shall create, test and maintain an AI system incident management plan and an AI system recovery plan.
items.why: Source of the quotation. Voluntary code. Also requires an audit trail to support incident response (2.3), support for end-users during and after an incident, agreed in contracts (10.3), and logging to support incident investigations (12.1).

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section D: Incident planning, response and recovery, Actions 1 to 4
items.quote: at least annual exercising of the plan involving relevant internal and external stakeholders
items.why: What boards are asked to assure: a plan, yearly exercising, personal responsibility for regulatory reporting during an incident, and a post-incident review that feeds lessons back. Voluntary; designed for medium and large organisations.

items.title: Incident management. Plan: Your cyber incident response processes
items.locator: Sections 'Developing an Incident Response (IR) plan', 'Incident Management (IM)' and 'Playbooks and regulatory issues'; page 3 of 7, version 1.0
items.quote: Keeping a careful record of the incident response, decisions made, actions taken, data captured (or missing) is incredibly useful for post-incident reviews.
items.why: The standard UK guidance on what a response plan contains: contacts, escalation criteria, a process for the full life-cycle, guidance on legal and regulatory requirements, and playbooks for specific incident types. Written in 2019 for cyber incidents; it does not mention AI, so AI failure types have to be added as playbooks.

items.title: Cyber Assessment Framework, Principle D2: Lessons learned
items.locator: Principle D2 statement and guidance; version 4.0, reviewed 6 August 2025
items.quote: When an incident occurs, steps are taken to understand its causes and to ensure remediating action is taken to protect against future incidents.
items.why: The standard for the learning loop: address root causes, keep records detailed enough to show how decisions were made, and feed lessons into protection and response plans. The framework is written for organisations running essential functions; it is a benchmark for others, not a duty.

items.title: Cyber security breaches survey 2025/2026
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Home Office
items.quote: Formal incident response plans were less widespread (25% of businesses; 19% of charities)
items.why: Source of the figure. Section 5.1 adds that 45% of businesses and 54% of charities had none of the listed measures, and that plans were 'largely untested or incomplete' in the qualitative interviews. The survey is about cyber security incidents, not AI failures.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 73: Reporting of serious incidents
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: Providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market shall report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities
items.why: International comparator. The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page). The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI and the text shown is not yet updated, so the brief gives no reporting windows and no application date. The duty is on providers; Article 26(5) on the same site has deployers inform the provider first.

items.title: PS26/2: Operational incident and third party reporting
items.quote: created single FCA, PRA and Bank of England regulatory regimes for operational incident and third party reporting
items.why: Sector rule for regulated financial firms: a standard incident report and a register of material third party arrangements, applying from 18 March 2027. The page notes that third parties now supply services by means of AI. Only the summary page was read, not the full policy statement.

items.title: Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS
items.locator: Summary, paragraphs 9 and 10; Part Three, paragraph 3.3. HC 414, Session 2017-2019
items.quote: had not tested the plan at a local level. This meant the NHS was not clear what actions it should take when affected by WannaCry
items.why: Official audit finding on what an unrehearsed plan is worth: a response plan existed but had never been exercised locally, so it was unclear who should lead and communications failed. The cover is dated 25 April 2018; the report is signed 24 October 2017. A cyber attack on the NHS in 2017, not an AI failure.

items.title: Capita fined £14m for data breach affecting over 6m people
items.locator: Sections 'The cyber attack' and 'Summary of the contraventions'
items.quote: Capita took 58 hours to respond appropriately, against a target response time of one hour.
items.why: Enforcement decision that turns on detection-to-response time: an alert was raised within ten minutes but the device was not quarantined for 58 hours; the security operations centre was understaffed. The regulator's statement was read, not the full penalty notice. Settled by agreement; a cyber attack, not an AI system.

items.title: The Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018, regulation 11: The duty to notify incidents
items.quote: without undue delay and in any event no later than 72 hours after the operator is aware that a NIS incident has occurred
items.why: A second binding reporting window to map beforehand, separate from the data protection one: operators of essential services must notify their competent authority of an incident with a significant impact on continuity of the service. Applies only to designated operators of essential services (regulation 12 covers digital service providers). The page showed no known outstanding effects; a Bill to reform these Regulations was before Parliament and no Act was found on legislation.gov.uk on the date checked.

items.title: Towards a common reporting framework for AI incidents
items.locator: Abstract and Executive summary; OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 34
items.quote: learn from AI harms identified elsewhere in the world
items.why: International comparator. Sets out 29 criteria for describing an AI incident so that reports can be compared across countries; useful as a template for what an internal AI incident record should capture. A policy paper, not a binding instrument; it creates no duty to report.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 4 (MANAGE function), MANAGE 4.3; also MANAGE 4.1 and, in Table 1, GOVERN 4.3
items.quote: Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities.
items.why: The AI-specific standard for the response and learning loop: incidents and errors are tracked, responded to, recovered from and documented, and the people affected are told. Voluntary; a United States framework.

items.title: Preventing Repeated Real World AI Failures by Cataloging Incidents: The AI Incident Database
items.quote: Intelligent systems currently cause real world harms without a collective memory of their failings.
items.why: The research case for the learning loop: without incident records, organisations repeat the same failures. Describes a public database of more than 1,000 incident reports. Preprint of a paper accepted to the Innovative Applications of Artificial Intelligence conference (IAAI-21); descriptive, not an evaluation of any response process.

items.title: Lessons for Editors of AI Incidents from the AI Incident Database
items.publisher: arXiv (Paeth, Atherton, Pittaras, Frase and McGregor)
items.quote: epistemic uncertainty in AI incident reporting is unavoidable
items.why: Reviews more than 750 recorded AI incidents and finds that cause, extent of harm and severity are often unclear when an incident is logged. Supports writing incident processes that work with incomplete facts. Preprint, not peer reviewed in the version read; based on publicly reported incidents only.

items.title: AI incident reporting: Addressing a gap in the UK's regulation of AI
items.locator: Summary page, section 'The need for incident reporting'
items.quote: the UK’s regulation of AI currently lacks an effective incident reporting framework
items.why: A UK policy institute's analysis, consistent with the brief's statement that no UK law sets a general duty to report AI failures. Recommends that government report incidents in its own use of AI. A think-tank report, not peer reviewed and not official; only the summary page was read.
